title: Culture & Intercultural Competence

pts: Teaching English inevitably teaches cultural assumptions embedded in the language's typical examples and framing.
Left unconscious, this defaults to whatever culture the materials happen to represent, often without scrutiny.
Making cultural content a deliberate teaching choice, rather than an accident of materials, is the goal here.

items: Choose one coursebook unit.
List every name, place, food, festival, custom and situation in it.
For each, note which culture it comes from.
Ask: is this choice deliberate? Is anything assumed to be ‘normal’?
Decide on one deliberate addition or change.
Do the same audit with your own board examples from a week of teaching.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

lines: Names: Tom, Sarah, Mr Brown. Food: sandwiches, fish and chips. Weather: rain in London. Holiday: Christmas.

blocks.x: Nothing here is wrong. But if it is all learners see, they learn that English belongs somewhere else. A deliberate addition might be a reading about a food stall in Hyderabad, a conversation between a Kenyan and a Korean engineer, and a festival calendar that includes Onam, Eid and Lunar New Year.

body: Purpose: to show that language carries culture. Content: a large English word ‘breakfast’ with a transparent layer lifting off it to reveal different breakfast plates from around the world (idli and chutney, toast and eggs, congee, injera). Style: warm, food-illustration style. Board version: a word with several small drawings around it.

items: None needed; this is an audit task.

blocks.x: A simple tally table on paper.

pts: English belongs to no single culture — avoid presenting one English-speaking country as the automatic cultural reference point.
This previews Tier IV's World Englishes strand, which treats global variety as the norm, not an exception.
Audit materials for this default explicitly; it's rarely a deliberate choice, just an unexamined one.

v: 20 minutes per lesson over a week
Short texts or images from different countries

items: Choose a theme (school, weddings, street food, greetings).
Collect short texts, images or videos from several places where English is used, including India.
In groups, learners read or watch one example and note what is similar to and different from their own experience.
Groups report to the class.
Conclude together: there is no single ‘English-speaking’ way.
Include examples from Nigeria, Singapore, the Philippines, Ireland and Jamaica, as well as the UK and USA.
Support: images with short captions; a sentence frame for reporting.
Challenge: learners find and present their own example.

lines: In ______, people usually ______. In my family, we ______.
This is similar to ______ because ______.
I was surprised that ______.

body: Purpose: to replace a single cultural centre with many. Content: a world map with many small glowing points connected by lines, rather than one bright centre. Style: modern, network-like. Board version: a circle of dots joined by lines.

items: StoryWeaver (free), which includes stories from many countries and in Indian English.

pts: The realistic goal is not imitating a native culture, but communicating effectively across cultural difference.
This reframes 'cultural competence' as a communicative skill in its own right, alongside grammar and vocabulary.
It applies equally to learners who will mostly use English with other non-native speakers, which is most learners today.
points.who: Michael Byram's Intercultural Communicative Competence model

v: A short story of a cross-cultural misunderstanding

items: Give learners a short story in which two people from different cultures misunderstand each other.
Learners describe what happened, without judging.
In groups, they suggest how each person might have interpreted the situation.
They propose what either person could have said or done to clear up the confusion.
Discuss: what did you need to know, and what did you need to do?
Learners write their own critical incident from experience (moving between states, visiting relatives, online gaming).
Support: provide possible interpretations for learners to choose from.

lines: Arjun, working in Germany, was invited to a colleague’s house for 7 p.m. He arrived at 7.40 with sweets. His colleague seemed annoyed. Arjun didn’t understand why.
What did Arjun expect? What did his colleague expect? What could Arjun say when he arrives? What could the colleague say?

blocks.x: This develops Byram’s skills of interpreting and relating: seeing an event from more than one perspective.

body: Purpose: to show interpretation. Content: two people looking at the same clock; one thought bubble shows ‘7 means 7’, the other shows ‘7 means sometime after 7’. Style: light, humorous, not mocking either person. Board version: two stick figures, one clock, two bubbles.

items: Padlet (free tier) for learners to post incident interpretations.

body: Jenny Thomas (1983) called communication failures of this kind pragmatic failure. She distinguished between failures caused by language (such as translating a politeness formula directly) and failures caused by different social assumptions (such as what counts as a small favour). Both are common, and neither is the fault of one side alone.

pts: Politeness norms, directness and turn-taking vary by culture and need explicit attention, not just correct grammar.
A grammatically perfect utterance can still cause real offence or confusion if its pragmatic register is wrong.
Pragmatics deserves the same explicit teaching attention Unit 6 gives grammar, not an assumption it'll be picked up incidentally.

items: Give learners three versions of a request, from very direct to very indirect.
Learners rank them from most to least polite.
Discuss which version suits which situation (friend, teacher, stranger, manager).
Learners role-play requests in different situations, choosing a suitable form.
Compare with how requests are made in learners’ home languages.
Do the same for refusals, apologies or compliments.
Support: provide the three forms on cards.
Challenge: add softeners (just, possibly, a bit).

lines: Give me your notes.
Can you give me your notes?
I was wondering if I could possibly borrow your notes for a day?
A: Could you lend me your pen?
B: Sure, here you are.

blocks.x: Many Indian languages use honorific verb forms and pronouns to show respect (as in Hindi āp and Kannada nīvu). English has no such pronoun system, and relies more on modal verbs, question forms and softeners. Learners who notice this difference can transfer their strong sense of politeness into English forms.

body: Purpose: to show degrees of directness. Content: a volume-style dial with three settings, labelled with the three example requests, from ‘direct’ to ‘very polite’, with small figures (friend, teacher, stranger) placed along it. Style: clear, simple. Board version: a line from ‘direct’ to ‘polite’ with the sentences written along it.

items: Flip or any video app for recording role-plays, where available and permitted.

pts: Critically evaluate coursebook cultural content for reductive, outdated, or one-dimensional representations.
This extends Unit 13's coursebook audit specifically to cultural content, which is often the least scrutinised part of a book.
Where materials fall short, supplement with more current or more varied cultural representation.

items: Show learners a text or picture that represents a group of people.
Learners ask: Who is shown? Who is missing? What are people doing? Is anyone reduced to a single characteristic?
Groups note any reductive or outdated representations.
Groups suggest how the material could be improved.
Where possible, bring in a more current or varied text.
Audit how India is represented in international coursebooks, or how other countries are represented in Indian textbooks.
Support: provide the questions as a checklist.

lines: Who speaks? Who is silent?
Are people shown in a range of roles?
Is a whole country shown through one image (e.g. elephants, the Taj Mahal, snake charmers)?
Is this how people there would describe themselves?

blocks.x: John Gray (2010) shows how global coursebooks have tended to present a narrow, aspirational picture of life: young, urban, well-off and mobile.

body: Purpose: to contrast a stereotype with a varied representation. Content: a single postcard image on the left (a generic ‘India’ with a camel and a palace) and on the right a collage of everyday scenes: a software office, a farm, a cricket match, a classroom, a metro station. Style: respectful, photographic collage feel. Board version: not applicable.

items: None needed; this is a critical reading task.

pts: Invite learners to share their own cultural perspectives, rather than positioning them only as recipients of target-culture information.
This is especially valuable in multilingual, multicultural classrooms where learners themselves are a rich resource.
It also directly supports rapport and engagement, connecting to Unit 22's climate-building principles.

items: Choose a theme (a festival, a family meal, a wedding custom, a game).
Learners prepare to explain one custom from their family or community.
In pairs, they explain and ask each other questions.
Selected learners share with the class.
Record new words on a class wall.
Invite a family member to speak (in English or with interpretation).
Support: a frame with guiding questions.
Challenge: learners compare two customs.

lines: In my family, we celebrate ______. We usually ______. The most important part is ______. My favourite part is ______.
Why do you do that? Who takes part? Is it the same in other families?

blocks.x: No learner should be asked to represent a whole community. Ask about their experience, not what ‘all’ people of a group do.

body: Purpose: to show learners as cultural informants. Content: learners in a circle, each with a small speech bubble containing a different symbol (a lamp, a kite, a drum, a plate of food), and arrows showing talk going in all directions. Style: joyful, inclusive. Board version: a circle of names with lines between them.

items: Canva (free for education) for a class ‘cultures’ poster.

points.h: English as a Lingua Franca, Culturally
points.sub: Most interactions involve no native speaker
pts: Most English interactions today happen between speakers who don't share a first language, often with no native speaker present at all.
This makes intercultural competence between non-native speakers more immediately relevant than native-culture knowledge for many learners.
Ties directly to Unit 4's Lingua Franca Core — intelligibility and mutual accommodation matter more than any single cultural or accent standard.

v: Recordings of speakers of English from different countries

items: Play short recordings of speakers of English from several countries (with no native speaker present).
Learners note words or phrases they found hard to understand, and what helped.
Discuss strategies used: repetition, rephrasing, checking, slowing down.
Learners role-play a problem-solving task and practise the strategies.
Set up an online exchange with a school in another country, where permitted.
Support: a list of repair phrases.

lines: Sorry, could you say that again?
Do you mean ______?
Let me put it another way.
So, what you’re saying is ______?

blocks.x: Research on English as a lingua franca suggests that successful speakers adapt to each other rather than to a native model (Jenkins 2000; Seidlhofer 2011).

body: Purpose: to show mutual accommodation. Content: two speakers from different countries on either side of a bridge, both walking towards the middle, with small speech bubbles showing ‘Do you mean…?’ and ‘Let me say it another way.’ Style: friendly, balanced. Board version: two figures and a bridge.

items: ePals or similar exchange platforms, subject to school policy [VERIFY current availability].

blocks.x: Recordings downloaded in advance, or teacher and colleague role-plays.

pts: Cultural and political topics can enrich a lesson but need careful, respectful framing appropriate to the specific group.
What's safely discussable varies significantly by context — assess the room rather than applying a fixed rule.
When in doubt, favour framings that invite multiple perspectives over ones that assume a single correct view.

v: A text on a debatable issue

items: Before the lesson, consider the group: which topics could cause distress or conflict?
Agree ground rules for discussion with the class.
Present the topic with several perspectives, not one.
Learners discuss in small groups, using the language of perspective.
Close by summarizing the range of views without judging who is right.
Use a ‘perspectives map’ in which learners place different views on a chart.
Support: offer an option to write a response rather than speak.

lines: Some people think ______, while others believe ______.
From one point of view, ______. On the other hand, ______.
I can see why someone might say ______.
Listen fully. Disagree with ideas, not people. Nobody has to share personal experiences.

body: Purpose: to show multiple perspectives. Content: a house with several windows, each showing a different view of the same garden. Style: calm, balanced. Board version: a square with several smaller squares, each labelled with a view.

items: Mentimeter (free tier) for anonymous opinions.

body: Next time you plan a lesson, change one example so that it comes from a place where English is used as a second or international language. Notice whether learners respond differently.

dek: Unit 24 of 100: English belongs to no single culture — teaching it well means building the competence to communicate across difference, not to imitate one native template.

aims.x: This unit considers what it means to teach culture in an English classroom when English belongs to no single culture. It moves the focus from knowledge about one ‘target culture’ to the skills of communicating across difference.
By the end of this unit you should be able to:

items: explain why teaching a language always involves teaching culture;
audit materials for a single-culture default;
describe intercultural communicative competence;
teach pragmatic features such as requests, refusals and politeness explicitly;
evaluate materials for stereotype;
use learners’ own cultural knowledge as a resource;
relate intercultural competence to English as a lingua franca;
handle sensitive topics with care.

why: Why this matters. Language teaching inevitably teaches cultural assumptions, whether the teacher intends it or not. Making that conscious is the difference between reflection and default.

background.x: For much of the twentieth century, ‘teaching culture’ in English classes meant teaching facts about Britain or the United States: their festivals, their food, their famous people. That approach made some sense when the purpose of learning English was assumed to be visiting or dealing with those countries. It makes much less sense today. Braj Kachru’s (1985) model of three circles of English, the inner, outer and expanding, drew attention to the fact that English is used as a home, national or official language in many countries, India among them, and as an international language almost everywhere. Most conversations in English now take place between people for whom it is not a first language (Seidlhofer 2011).

Culture has not become less important as a result. It has become more complex. Claire Kramsch (1993) argues that language and culture cannot be separated: every choice of word, example and topic carries cultural meaning. Michael Byram (1997) proposed a model of intercultural communicative competence, which includes attitudes of curiosity and openness, knowledge of how social groups work, skills of interpreting and relating, skills of discovery and interaction, and critical cultural awareness. The aim is not to make learners into imitation Britons or Americans but to make them skilled mediators between cultures, including their own.

Indian classrooms are already intercultural. Learners may come from different linguistic, religious and regional backgrounds, and the NCF 2023 encourages classrooms that value this diversity (NCERT 2023). English, used well, can be a language in which learners talk about their own lives and learn about others’, without any culture being treated as the default.

items: Pragmatic appropriateness. Assess role-plays for suitable choice of request or apology form, as well as accuracy.
Intercultural reflection. A short written response to a critical incident, assessed for the ability to see more than one perspective.
Materials audit. Learners present an evaluation of a text for stereotype, with suggested improvements.
Repair strategies. Observe whether learners use clarification and rephrasing strategies in lingua franca tasks.
Which culture is the default in your teaching materials? Is that a deliberate choice?
How often do learners share their own cultural knowledge in your lessons?
How do you teach politeness in English? Do you compare it with learners’ home languages?
How would you respond if a learner made a stereotyped remark in class?
Which topics do you avoid, and why?

terms.def: The ability to evaluate critically the practices and values of one’s own and other cultures, a key element of intercultural communicative competence (Byram 1997).
An event, often small, that prompts reflection and learning; in intercultural learning, a brief case of misunderstanding between people from different cultures.
A learner who shares knowledge of their own culture, customs or community with the class, treating learners’ experiences as a resource for intercultural learning.

English used as a shared language between speakers who have different first languages, such as an Indian and a Japanese engineer. Research focuses on mutual intelligibility rather than conformity to native-speaker norms (Seidlhofer 2011).
The ability to communicate effectively and appropriately with people from other cultures, combining language skills with attitudes, knowledge and skills of interpreting and relating (Byram 1997).

A model of World Englishes with three concentric circles: the Inner Circle, where English is a native language; the Outer Circle, including India, where it is a second language; and the Expanding Circle (Kachru 1985).
The ways language users show consideration for others and manage social relationships, such as through forms of address, indirectness and hedging.

The inability to understand or convey intended meaning because language, though grammatically correct, is inappropriate to the context or relationship, such as an overly direct request to a senior officer (Thomas 1983).

The study of how meaning depends on context, speakers’ intentions and social relationships, including speech acts, politeness and implied meaning; for example, how ‘It’s cold in here’ can function as a request.

A fixed, oversimplified generalization about a group of people, applied to every member. In intercultural teaching, learners examine stereotypes, including those in materials, and learn to see individuals and diversity within cultures.
